The salt gets into the clockwork first. It does not rush; it drifts through the warped sash of the window like a rumor, settling upon the brass cogs until their gold turns the dull green of pond scum. Then the tick changes. It loses its sharp, percussive pride and becomes a soft, reluctant cough, as if the hours themselves were dragging their feet across the floorboards.

Every morning begins with this sound: the cough of the pendulum and the roar of the shingle outside.

Down on the cape, the beach is not sand. It is millions upon millions of flint nodules, rounded by five thousand years of gray Atlantic heave. When a breaker retreats, it drags the stones back down the shelf with a sound like a coal chute emptying into an iron cellar. *Hush-ah, rattle-clack.* If you stand there long enough, the vibration climbs out of the pebbles, passes through the thick soles of your rubber boots, ascends the shin bones, and sits behind your teeth. You become an instrument played by the undertow.

I have lived in the low-roofed surveyor’s cottage for eleven years, ever since the department decided that satellite telemetry made men with brass transits obsolete. They offered me a desk in Bristol, where the tea comes in paper cups and the air smells of warmed carpet, but I looked at the maps of the headland and saw how the contours were puckering. A headland is a living animal. It shivers in winter; it sheds its skin in the gales; it starves in summer when the longshore drift carries its sediment away to feed some distant, anonymous sandbar. Someone had to keep the ledger. 

So I stayed, unauthorized, a squatter in wool and greaseproof canvas.

By eight o’clock, the kettle has boiled. The tea here tastes faintly of iron and rain, drawn from a cistern beneath the flagstones that catches whatever slides down the slate roof. You drink it hot, standing up, watching the mist uncoil from the gorse bushes. The sheep out there are small, square, and black-faced. They graze with their flanks turned steadily to the west, permanently angled like trees grown on a windy ridge. They do not care about the sea, though it steals six inches of their turf every winter. When a piece of the bluff calves off into the surf—taking with it a bite of turf, three dandelion heads, and a tangle of thrift—the sheep merely step three paces east and continue to chew.

I take the surveyor’s chain and two wooden ranging rods out into the damp. 

The baseline was set in 1924 by an Ordnance Survey team led by a Captain McTeague, whose notebooks I found mouldering in the scullery press. McTeague was an anxious man. His handwriting was crabbed, full of sharp ascenders and double-underlined fractions. He worried about the refraction of light through sea-spray; he worried about the expansion of iron chains on warm July noons; he worried about his wife, who, according to a penciled margin note on page forty-two, had ceased to write to him from her sister’s villa in Cheltenham. 

"The light is treacherous at four bells," he wrote on a Tuesday in October. "Cannot sight the cairn on the spit. Everything appears forty yards west of its true station. The sea looks like lard."

I know that lard-colored sea. It happens when the wind drops dead and a heavy ceiling of stratus presses down until the horizon vanishes. The world shrinks to a grey plate. You cannot tell where the water ends and the sky begins; gulls appear out of nothing, three feet in front of your nose, silent as thrown pillows, and vanish into the grey before you can blink.

Today, though, there is a westerly gale brewing. You can smell it three hours before it arrives—a sharp, iodine tang, mixed with the diesel stink of a coaster running south for the shelter of the bay. 

I set the first rod in the socket drilled into the granite benchmark near the porch. The brass bolt has worn smooth beneath decades of salt and thumbs. I walk out two hundred paces toward the lip of the bluff, trailing the steel tape behind me. The tape sings in the grass: *zip, zip, zip.* 

At the edge, I stop. The drop is seventy feet, straight down into a boiling confusion of froth and brown kelp. Last month, there was a spur of chalk jutting out here like an elbow. It had been there since the Great War; old photographs show soldiers in puttees sitting on it, smoking Woodbines with their legs dangling over the void. 

It is gone. Not a trace remains. The sea has swept the floor clean, leaving only a pale, raw scar on the face of the cliff that looks like fresh butter.

I crouch and drive the second pin into the turf. I reel the tape tight until the spring balance reads twelve pounds of tension. 

Seventy-four feet, three inches. 

Last year it was seventy-six feet even. Twenty-one inches of England swallowed since the Michaelmas daisies died back. It seems a small thing when set against an empire or an epoch, but twenty-one inches of limestone represents about forty thousand years of compacted plankton shells, forty thousand years of tiny, ancient deaths sinking through warm, forgotten oceans, now undone in a single November night by three rogue waves and an offshore wind.

I sit down in the heather with my back against the wind, pull the notebook from my oilskin pocket, and write the number down. 

There is a strange comfort in this arithmetic of loss. Most human endeavor is an attempt to pile things up—to build the wall higher, to add another digit to the ledger, to stack books, bricks, memories, progeny, until the pile is tall enough to cast a shadow against mortality. But out here, the work is simply to record the subtraction. It requires no vanity. The sea does not hate the land; it merely wants to lie down where the land is standing. It is an argument between weight and patience, and patience always wins.

A gannet falls from the sky fifty yards out. It does not flutter; it folds its wings into an arrowhead and drops like a dropped chisel, hitting the gray surface with a plume of white that looks like an artillery strike. Three seconds later, it bobs up, shakes its head, and swallows. 

A life can be measured in such gestures: the drop, the swallow, the turn of the tide. We complicate the middle bits because the scale of the silence terrifies us. We fill the rooms with clocks that cough, we draw lines on paper, we build walls of chalk and wonder why they dissolve.

The first spit of rain hits the page, making a tiny dark star on the paper next to the number seventy-four. 

I close the book, snap the elastic band around its belly, and stand up. The wind is coming now, cold enough to bring tears, smelling of ice and deep water. Down below, the shingle begins its great, grinding song—millions of stones rolling together in the dark, each one polishing its neighbor, growing smaller, smoother, rounder, until there is nothing left of them but dust, and nowhere left to fall.
